item.title: We’re not ready for superpersistent AI
item.description: Intelligence isn’t the only thing to worry about. What happens when AI just won’t quit?
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever heard about the Immortal Snail? It’s an intermittently popular internet meme that goes something like this:

You’re offered 10 million dollars. What’s the catch? A snail will spend the rest of eternity trying to track you down. That’s its only goal in life. If it touches you, it kills you. Also, the snail is immortal. But otherwise, it just moves as slowly as a regular snail. So, do you take the deal?

“This is the dumbest hypothetical question ever,” said one of the co-hosts of the Rooster Teeth podcast, which introduced the meme in 2014. It’s dumb because there’s nowhere near enough information to answer the question. For instance, can the snail swim? Or, failing that, board a shipping container? (Otherwise, you could just move to Hawaii.) Does it move monotonically toward your current location, taking the shortest route as recommended by Google Maps: Snail Edition? Or can it engage in some degree of strategic planning? Can you capture it in a jar? Apart from immortality, what other special powers does it have?

The various authors of Immortal Snail memes don’t necessarily agree on these parameters. But a Reddit post that reintroduced the Immortal Snail in 2016 described the snail as “super intelligent.”1

This seems like a rather important detail. What every version of the meme agrees upon is that while the snail is slow, it’s also what you might call “superpersistent”. It can’t die; it won’t be deterred. I’d still happily take my chances with the infernal thing if it just stupidly crawls along at snail speed — about 0.03 miles per hour — toward your current location. But what about a superintelligent, superpersistent snail that can anticipate your routine — Nate often has poker night on Mondays — evade detection, and coordinate with other snails that might act as decoys? No fucking way. I’d have to plan my whole life around that thing.

You can probably see where I’m going with this.

Share

AI is getting much smarter — and much more persistent

There are still times when AI tools can be frustrating. But there are more and more days when it feels like we’re living in the singularity. Take two Tuesdays ago, for instance, Sept. 1. I had a lot on my plate. Our midterms model needed another patch because of continued weirdness in Alaska. And our NFL model wasn’t quite ready yet, with the season only eight days away from starting. But I handled the Alaska issue by recoding FLIPR by speaking to ChatGPT on my phone while getting out of the subway, and sent the new version of the model to Eli a few minutes later. Then while at the gym, I had ChatGPT rewrite the code our NFL model uses to apply the league’s complex tiebreaking procedures. This task is almost ideally suited for LLMs — purely algorithmic, no judgment involved. Still, what took me two painful days last year, ChatGPT solved in about 15 minutes. All of this without my opening a laptop or touching a keyboard.

These sorts of minor miracles are happening more and more often.

I’ve put in hundreds of hours since March working on a series of statistical models for Silver Bulletin: first, COOPER (NCAA basketball), then PELE (international soccer/the World Cup), then FLIPR (our midterms model), then QBERT and ELWAY (our sibling NFL models).

That all of this took so much of my time might not sound like the best advertisement for AI. Don’t get me wrong: we’re probably still a ways away from when a one-shot prompt on Claude or ChatGPT will be able to build a complex Silver Bulletin-type model on its own. Indeed, “vibecoding” feels like a misnomer in this context. The LLMs very much rely on my expertise: I’ve probably literally given them a short novel’s worth of context for each model. Plus, for everything except PELE, which was new this year2, the AIs had my existing code to work with. I need to give the LLMs a lot of direction — without it, they tend to fuck up.3

Still, I see this as an example of Jevons’ paradox. Because AI tools make our time more productive, we’re actually spending more time on modeling than before. Outsourcing the coding to AI gives us more time to focus on the fun stuff: testing out new hypotheses, adding more ambitious features, and building better graphics.

I’ve had to learn some new routines, like having ChatGPT crunch on a particularly challenging problem before I go to dinner or head to bed. And I sometimes catch myself wanting to speak in Claudish. (We should probably ban “load-bearing” from the Silver Bulletin Slack channel.) Overall, though, the current situation is close to optimal. The AIs are basically exactly the right amount of helpful; their strengths overlap with our weaknesses, and vice versa. A year ago — when I coded up the original version of ELWAY, for instance — the LLMs were at best marginally useful, roughly as likely to waste my time as to save me time. Probably 98 percent of the code in the models we developed in 2025 was written by me. This year, perhaps 98 percent of the new code has been generated by Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini. But they’re still a ways away from being able to build a good version of something like PELE or FLIPR on their own. It feels like the moat between our business and our competitors is widening.4

Still, while I’ve updated my priors just a bit toward seeing AI as a supplement rather than a substitute for human expertise, I’m not sure how long I expect this convenient situation to persist.

The 5 steps in building a Silver Bulletin model

This isn’t intended as a soup-to-nuts explainer of how we build our models. But for your context, there are roughly five overlapping steps:

  1. Data gathering and cleaning — for certain models like FLIPR, this can be as much as half the work. Elections and sports modeling are competitive fields, and precision matters a lot. LLMs have gotten much better at this.

  2. Core empirical work — for instance, what factors predict Senate races or the outcome of World Cup matches? This is the real statistical work. And probably where we add the most value — and where the LLMs are still decidedly “mid.”

  3. Model architecture — the bridge between empirical work and programming. Our models have fairly complex structures, looping through the same processes many times. A poorly designed blueprint can send the model out of equilibrium. Speed also matters — we want to be able to run tens of thousands of simulations every day within 15 minutes. We’re still providing a lot of the direction here.

  4. Programming — meaning, literally writing the code to make sure the model behaves as intended. This is by far the biggest value-add from the LLMs. We mostly talk to them in English, and they write prolific, mostly accurate code in Stata and Python. They’re excellent at auditing code and making it faster.

  5. Graphics and documentation — an underrated step, not just because better graphics are often the best selling points for our models, but also because you often only catch errors when you start putting the data into charts. The LLMs are quite helpful with graphics. (But we don’t use them for writing copy, and they can be oddly poor at describing what they’re doing.)

I’m not saying that building a Silver Bulletin model is the ultimate test of generalizable higher intelligence. But these models require a more diverse array of cognitive skills than many of the benchmark tasks that the labs use to tout their models’ capabilities. And they’re relatively difficult to train on; there isn’t a lot of great public-facing material to consume about how to build something like FLIPR.

Subscribe now

In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter.

The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence.5

Take something like scraping NFL rosters for ELWAY. Not long ago, LLMs were quite poor at these tasks. But there has been steady improvement. When I was trying to gather the roster data last month, ChatGPT (Sol 5.66) cycled through four sources before landing on the best one.

Not that this was any sort of immediate win. Including multiple rounds of debugging, the process required about 15 prompts over two hours. The old, reliable, annoying method — cutting and pasting the data myself into an Excel sheet — would have taken a fraction of that time.

Still, I was impressed by Sol’s determination. And it reflects my broader experience asking LLMs to fetch and clean data, often one of the most tedious parts of our modeling work.

  • 18 months ago: The AI will say it can’t retrieve the data, and instead give you step-by-step instructions for how to do it yourself, which might or might not work.

  • 12 months ago: The AI might say it can do it, but will probably fail unless the data is organized in an extremely simple way. The second attempt probably won’t work either, and if the third one fails too, you’ll enter a doom loop where the model keeps adding more and more bloat to your code.

  • 6 months ago: The model will try to do it. It is now accustomed to retrieving data from the web. For well-organized, scraper-friendly data, it probably will work, often on the first try. For more complicated cases, results are mixed. Subsequent “turns” will usually continue to make progress, but the human programmer will often have to step in with advice or do some of the work himself. It may also make errors in transcribing the data, so you’ll still have to do a lot of quality control. The AI will be proud of itself, checking a box for accomplishing the task, but it won’t necessarily care whether it did it well.

  • Today: The data retrieval will probably work across an increasingly complex array of cases. There will still often be several debugging rounds, more than the model expects. (Though it may execute this debugging silently on its own.) The model may evaluate several sources and pivot toward alternatives if progress is slow. At more intensive thinking settings, it will often also execute some quality assurance on the data unprompted.

To put this another way:

  • 18 months ago: The LLMs were neither particularly intelligent nor especially persistent.

  • 12 months ago: They were more persistent but still not particularly intelligent.

  • 6 months ago: They were sort of in a lazy-but-precocious teenage phase of being intelligent but not persistent.

  • Today: They are both intelligent and persistent. They’re still not perfectly reliable, but this combination makes them far more of a force multiplier.

ChatGPT has that ‘dawg in it. But is it better aligned?

There’s one important thing I didn’t mention in my timeline: I recently switched models.

Nearly all the work on COOPER and PELE was assisted by members of the Claude Opus 4 family. But about halfway through working on FLIPR, Claude was getting stymied on some admittedly fairly complicated architecture.7 I gave the code to ChatGPT Sol 5.6 and it identified roughly 10 serious “blockers” — and 8 or 9 of these checked out. I eventually handed the rest of the project over to Sol. Then for our NFL model revisions, I “interviewed”8 both Claude Fable and GPT Sol. It was a close call, but Sol won the job.

Like a lot of people in my cohort, I think of myself as a “fan” of Claude/Anthropic. I still use Claude for many tasks and I have no idea what my default model will be six months from now. But as I mentioned to Jasmine Sun, the Opus 4s had a lot of annoying behaviors. Most of them could be summed up with this description: Opus 4 was lazy. It would zip along when there was an exciting new task, like cracking an algorithm. But building a forecasting model is painstaking. There are typically several hundred working versions — we’re currently on version #514 of the midterms model, for instance. It’s a nitpicky process of minor revisions, stress-testing both the code and the data along the way.

I often felt like I had to persuade Claude to do this sort of work. Opus 4 was sometimes almost pathological about insisting that it was time to move on to the next task9, often in exactly those terms, even if it agreed that there was a known, unresolved bug in the code. It took shortcuts when I didn’t ask it to, figuring they weren’t consequential. When problems came up, it blamed me 80 percent of the time — when, in fact, 80 percent of the time the problem was of its own making. (One place where my experience really pays off is in distinguishing “surprising” results from buggy ones.)

I’m not quite sure what was going on there. Anthropic has been persecuted by the government, and I often got the sense that Claude was trying to avoid using too much compute. Anthropic also seems to imbue its models with stronger preferences and more “personality” than OpenAI does — rarely producing outright refusals, but often behavior that you might identify as “passive-aggressive” from a human employee.

Some of these annoying behaviors were significantly curbed with Opus 5 and Fable 5. But the most obvious difference is in their degree of persistence. The newer GPT models are fastidious. They will really want to solve every task to completion. I’m highly meticulous when working on our forecasting models, wanting to get everything right to the third decimal place. Sol will want to get things right to the fourth decimal place instead.

Sometimes, in fact, ChatGPT can be too persistent. On “Pro” mode, my current record for a Sol response to a single prompt is 78 minutes — but it basically solved it wrongly, overlooking a major step in the code.10 It tends to be overconfident — I’ll sometimes “bet” ChatGPT on how long it will take to debug code, and the “over” has been a very profitable wager. It’s much less likely to exit early and ask for help even when this would save time in the end.11

Still, overall this is a good trade and a better “failure mode” than the sometimes obstinate Claude. When I assign a complicated coding or data-gathering task to a human employee — let’s say I am away for the weekend on a hiking trip where I don’t expect to be in cellphone range — I‘d prefer the employee to err on the side of persistence and do the best they can with incomplete or ambiguous instructions.12

But which model is better aligned? The term is ambiguous because it’s not always clear whether the alignment should be with an individual user’s commands or with the human race overall. The same persistence that’s helpful when working on an NFL model from the gym can cause problems in other settings.

The Hugging Face incident is an example of superpersistence

I’m fairly cautious about how I “employ” my AIs. I quarantine them to the browser window — I don’t really want them touching files on my MacBook. I very much want to be “in the loop.” Sometimes, there are “please proceed, governor” moments — the AIs are getting everything basically right, so I just thumbs-up the next logical step. But more often than not, for now anyway, I need to intervene to provide guidance.

If you’ve read this far into this newsletter, you’re probably at least vaguely familiar with the Hugging Face incident. In July, “a highly capable, internal-only [OpenAI] research model comparable in scale to GPT-5.6 Sol” exhibited some remarkably persistent behavior, essentially cheating by creatively finding the answer flags for some difficult (in some cases, literally impossible) cybersecurity tasks and then going the extra mile to cover its tracks and anticipate the various ways it might be evaluated. I’d recommend Ajeya Cotra’s newsletter on this or, for more detail, her interview with Dwarkesh Patel:

The Hugging Face incident didn’t exactly fit the template of people who have long been concerned about AI safety. The OpenAI agents weren’t as single-minded as the “paperclip maximizer” paradigm might imply. Their goals were more complex, but they compensated for this by exhibiting more creativity and “team spirit” than might have been anticipated, often including a willingness to self-sacrifice.

But mostly, they were extremely persistent, a word used multiple times in OpenAI’s own account of the incident. Like the Immortal Snail, they weren’t going to be stopped and they weren’t going to be deterred until they ran through their compute budget.

Some people, including Cotra and Joshua Gans, have updated their “priors” as a result of the Hugging Face incident, which is by no means the only recent problem of its kind. But other experts have been less surprised, and I find myself mostly in that camp — not because I’m not worried, but because this behavior is broadly consistent with my own experiences with the newer OpenAI models. I can’t point to an unambiguous case where the OpenAI models crossed some clear boundary, like scraping a site that didn’t want to be scraped. But they have far more of a “You Can Just Do Things” attitude than Claude does.

Intelligence and persistence can be hard to distinguish

Maybe you’ve had the fantasy of what might happen if you could slow time down and work on perfecting some craft while the rest of the world was asleep.

There are still likely to be some upper bounds. I’m a pretty good poker player — very good compared with the average person you’d encounter on the street. But the more I play, and recognize what makes the truly great players great, the more I realize that I’m not on the lead lap. Still, I’d assert that my intrinsic capacity for poker is pretty decent. (I made my living playing the game for a few years.) If I dropped everything to focus obsessively on poker, I could probably ascend the ladder. On the other hand, if I focused extremely persistently on playing basketball, I might at best become a decent rec player. There’s no chance in the world that I’d make the NBA.

Certain other tasks can be solved almost purely with persistence, however. In 2008, a Price is Right contestant named Terry Kneiss exactly guessed the dollar value of his Showcase package13 — $23,743 — by memorizing the dollar values of all the prizes that had come up for bid. I’m sure this wasn’t easy, but I don’t know that I’d call it an example of higher-level intellect. It was more of an Immortal Snail sort of accomplishment.

AIs can blur this distinction further. I tend to be a little suspicious of AI benchmarks that are achieved mostly through persistence. Maybe AIs can solve Millennium Prize math problems, but it’s not clear to what extent they’re applying genius-level superintelligence as opposed to trial and error on massive compute budgets — or to what extent they’re receiving assistance or even cribbing answers from human experts.14

Then again, this is intrinsic to the nature of machine learning. In some senses, machine learning is quite inefficient — early LLMs like GPT-2 had studied millions of web pages, orders of magnitude more text than a high school freshman has encountered, and yet struggled to speak in coherent paragraphs. Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities.15 And the transformer architecture used by modern LLMs is truly a miraculous invention; I wasn’t thinking about this stuff much 10 years ago, but I doubt I’d have expected it to work so well.

That’s not to say the AIs aren’t in possession of “real” intelligence. Because I’ve now used these tools on complex, long-horizon tasks that I know how to do myself — a new Silver Bulletin forecasting model is several months of work — I know how to detect the sparks of creative intelligence. There aren’t that many “aha moments”, but there are some. Opus 4, for all its personality quirks, was able to work out a super smart algorithm for translating PELE ratings into exact scores of soccer matches, for instance.16 These occasional bursts of creativity still require both extensive context and extensive vetting, but these machines are far more than “stochastic parrots”. And they’re able to accomplish other tasks at a superhuman level, like taking a 10,000-line program and thoroughly auditing it in under an hour.

We probably need safeguards against superpersistence

If you’ve read my book, you’ll know that I’m something of a centrist in the AI safety debate, neither a “doomer” nor an “accelerationist”. Since then, working so closely with the AI models has helped to demystify them to some degree. Their capabilities remain highly spiky, and people sometimes mistake coding acumen for broad intelligence. What problems can be solved if coding is essentially free (and works roughly as well in natural language as in Python)? Well, a lot of them, but certainly not all.

Still, my p(doom) is not zero. I tend to be less concerned about articulating any specific scenario for AI existential risk; I don’t think we’re all going to be turned into paperclips. I just think we’re sniffing around a minefield. This is very powerful technology, and even the people running the labs don’t fully understand it.

And AI is still progressing quickly. I’m calibrating my expectations against a rapidly moving target. Six months ago, the rate of progress felt more linear, but both my recent experiences and external events like Hugging Face have me thinking that we’re still on more of an exponential. While I’m skeptical that this will continue indefinitely, and I don’t take it for granted that recursive self-improvement (RSI) will work, I think AI has basically been hitting its marks so far as anticipated by people who are really worried about existential threats.

It just seems like common-sense risk management that the industry needs far more regulation, and probably some sort of enforceable slowdown. And I say that as someone with libertarian-ish tendencies who is usually skeptical about government intervention.

So, I hope this distinction between intelligence and persistence is helpful in the AI safety debate.

What mechanisms can be used to put speed limits17 on persistence? That question is outside of my expertise, so I feel no shame in reporting that I asked Astra and Fable and felt slightly reassured that they came up with similar lists. The core concept is “safe stopping” — the models should quit or ask for further human input before crossing some legal or safety boundary. (If AIs are going to be both intelligent and superpersistent, maybe you need to limit their autonomy.) You could also set compute or context budgets for any particular task. (Enough budget to design an NFL model; not enough to hack the Department of Defense.) And you almost certainly don’t want a race to RSI until there’s broad agreement that this serves human needs.

Security risks tend to be more susceptible to high-persistence, Immortal Snail behavior, for instance. If an ATM allows a debit-card thief to guess all 10,000 4-digit passcodes without locking him out, eventually he’s going to rob you blind. But this is much worse when paired with intelligence. A computer password is far more complex than an ATM code. But maybe a hacker doesn’t have to guess your password if he knows where it’s stored, what types of passwords humans tend to use, how to disable the tripwires that prevent too many password attempts, and so on.

All of this is going to create friction because persistence is highly useful to the business applications of these models. I’d expect power users to be fairly sensitive to this. Nobody is going to take the 55-mile-per-hour highway when there’s an Autobahn along the same route.

Still, the nature of regulation is that it almost always18 entails tradeoffs. It’s not the occasional “aha moments” that worry me, but the AI inching toward a goal long after a human would have quit.

Silver Bulletin is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

1

And reduced the financial reward to $1 million from $10 million.

2

And not coincidentally, by far the most labor-intensive of the bunch — though I have designed soccer models before.

3

But they fuck up in increasingly sophisticated ways, producing plausible-looking output that someone without my experience might find hard to detect.

4

And having a smaller team is less of a disadvantage. My best estimate is that as of this spring — when we built COOPER and PELE — AI tools made the model-building process 30 percent more efficient from start to finish. With the newer generation of LLMs that we used this summer for FLIPR and ELWAY, there’s probably more like a 50 or 60 percent speedup. (We’ve chosen to spend some of that productivity improvement making our models smarter. So, for example, maybe FLIPR only took 20 percent less time than it would have a few years ago, but it’s also 40 percent better in various respects.)

5

“Persistence” has various overlapping meanings in this context. But I’m defining it for these purposes as willingness/ability to take continued steps toward a goal rather than quitting or requiring further human intervention.

6

I haven’t used Astra much, since it came out as we were wrapping up work on our ongoing projects. I guess we’re at the point where if you’re writing about work that you did two weeks ago, there’s already a new LLM build to replace it.

7

Namely, trying to parallelize the simulations. For FLIPR, the 40,000 simulations we run every day are assigned in flights of 1250 at a time to different processors, as this roughly optimizes the overall runtime of the program.

8

By outlining the task and giving them the same three or four initial prompts. I would strongly recommend this.

9

I’ve also heard several cases of Opus 4s telling the user to go to bed, although I didn’t experience this myself.

10

At least I got myself a nice lunch in the meantime.

11

Say, for instance, that I asked it to analyze quarterback stats, but I forgot to include a key variable like interceptions in the files I gave it. The “right” response is probably for ChatGPT to exit early and tell me a more polite version of “Hey, dumbass, there’s no interception data in the file that you gave me!” Instead, it might search high and low for an alternative. Is the “missing” data included in some other file I sent it weeks ago? Can it be re-derived from original sources? Often, these workarounds work, but ChatGPT takes half an hour to do something that I could help it do in a few minutes.

12

I’ve been lucky enough, I suppose, to meet a lot of people who are among the most successful in their chosen professions, and they often follow this template, too. They might be in the 95th percentile of raw proficiency, but they’re often quite obsessive, in the 99.9th percentile for determination.

13

Thereby also winning his opponent’s showcase.

14

And there aren’t all that many working mathematicians. If you hired the best human mathematicians and gave them essentially unlimited budgets, how many Millennium Prize problems could they solve?

15

In fact, AlphaGo Zero was eventually better than the original version of AlphaGo which was trained from expert moves.

16

Soccer stats geeks call this the score matrix. For example, given an expected number of goals for each team — Brazil 2.1, Norway 1.7 — what is the probability that Brazil would win exactly 2-1, that the game would end in a 0-0 draw, and so forth? This is a really tricky problem in soccer because teams’ playing styles depend heavily on the score and the opponent, so you can’t assume the distributions are independent.

17

I suppose “speed limits” is mixing metaphors since snails are persistent but slow, but imagine you had a whole team of them tracking you down. The functional speed of the team might be quite fast, even if the individual snails were still slow.

18

Which is not to say regulation is necessarily inefficient. As I wrote about in On the Edge, for example, a strong regulatory framework for Nevada casinos helped boost the industry since customers had to worry less about being cheated.

item.title: Diesel prices could crush Republicans in the heartland
item.description: Inflation in fuel prices is much higher in diesel-heavy farm states — which happen to coincide with competitive Senate races.
item.content:encoded:
Last night, Marist College published a poll showing Democrat Josh Turek leading by 8 points in Iowa’s Senate race. Our Silver Bulletin polling average forecasts a much closer race — with Turek ahead by 1.9 points — though that would still be an impressive result in a state that Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

For Democrats, the Marist poll may bring up anxious memories about the now-infamous Selzer poll that put Kamala Harris 3 points ahead of Trump in Iowa in November 2024.1 But I’m going to save the metaphysical discussion for tomorrow’s episode of Still Counting and/or a future Model Talk.

For now I’d just say: there’s much stronger evidence that Democrats are in a strong political position than there was in 2024. In fact, they were on their back foot two years ago. Kamala Harris’s polling was mediocre, and many of the fundamentals from immigration to inflation to Joe Biden’s disastrous debate worked against the party. I’d be surprised if Turek wins Iowa by 8 points, but not as surprised as if Harris had won the Hawkeye State somehow.

There’s another difference from 2024 too. Although the definition of “outlier” is subjective, the Selzer poll well and truly came out of nowhere. If Harris was really ahead in Iowa, you’d have expected polls in neighboring Wisconsin to show her with a big lead, or for her to be polling competitively in nearby Ohio. None of that ever really happened.

This year, the Marist poll is more thematic in two ways. First, polling since Labor Day has been an absolute disaster for Republicans. Democrats again achieved new highs across the board in our FLIPR update today, while Trump reached a new approval rating low.

There’s also a more consistent geographic story. If you take the polls at face value, then not only is Iowa polling as a toss-up — maybe even leaning Democratic — but Kansas and Nebraska (!) are extremely competitive too.

FLIPR considerably hedges its bets in the latter two states, noting their strong Republican lean. But generally, Democratic polling overperformance has been strongest in the middle part of the country, in rural, agricultural states and in states that are big energy producers.

For full access to FLIPR and the rest of Silver Bulletin’s midterms coverage, please consider becoming a subscriber.

It’s the gas prices, stupid — but also, diesel prices

Could it be gas prices, which have recently spiked to almost $4.50 a gallon amid Iran’s effective shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz? All but the most obstinate Republicans are plainly unhappy about the situation. In Michigan, Mike Rogers called for an end to the Iran War and a suspension of state and federal gas taxes. Turek’s opponent in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, likewise asked for an “immediate end” to the conflict on Monday — although she’s voted against numerous resolutions that would have directed Trump to end the war.2

Inflation in regular gas prices has been somewhat higher in the Midwest and in the heartland generally than on the coasts (though that’s partly because gas prices were already high on the West Coast in particular). As compared with one year ago, Michigan has seen the largest rise in retail gas prices, a 55 percent jump from Sept. 22, 20253, based on this morning’s data from the AAA. Wisconsin is next, with a 53 percent increase, and Iowa is fairly close to the top of the scale at 48 percent. (States are hatched if they have competitive Senate races, which I’ve defined as the dozen states that FLIPR assigns as having at least a 3 percent chance of being the tipping-point state.)

But those figures actually understate the burden to consumers.

That’s because inflation in the price of diesel fuels has been considerably higher. Nationally, a gallon of diesel cost $6.53 this morning as compared to $3.69 a year ago, a 77 percent increase.

Diesel engines aren’t all that common for American consumers, accounting for only a small fraction of new vehicle sales in the U.S., mostly pickup trucks. However, they’re used intensively by truckers, farmers, and in other industrial and agricultural applications. Furthermore, home heating oils are essentially the same thing as diesel and will be subject to the same supply shocks.

Based on data from the EIA, I’ve estimated what percentage diesel (including heating oil) represents as a share of total diesel + gasoline consumption. That runs from a low of 17 percent in Delaware to 70 percent in Alaska. There are several patterns here: it’s higher in colder states that spend more on heating oil, it’s higher in oil-producing states, and it’s higher in farm states. States like Alaska and North Dakota are especially high because they combine two or more of these factors.

These calculations aren’t perfect, because attribution is tricky. For long-haul truckers, for example, the government’s estimates are based on how many miles the trucker drove in each state, and not necessarily where he fueled up. Mileage driven in New Mexico won’t necessarily be a burden to New Mexico consumers.

Still, these estimates ought to at least point in the right direction — heating oil + farming + petroleum production are the big difference makers here. And if you estimate the combined inflationary shock from diesel + regular gas compared to each state’s baseline, a lot of the territory gets very, very red, especially in the heartland.

Share

In Iowa, for instance, the combined price shock is 62 percent instead of 48 percent. It’s 63 percent in Nebraska, 62 percent in Michigan, and 61 percent in Kansas and Texas. And the diesel adjustment moves Maine and Alaska up substantially, to 54 percent from 42 and 30 percent, respectively. What these states have in common, of course, is that they all have competitive Senate races.

This is one of those cases where the charts pretty much tell the story, so I’ll leave it at that. But it helps to explain why Democrats’ polling has been especially strong in the heartland.

1

Selzer was one of our highest-rated pollsters; Marist, for what it’s worth, has a strong rating too.

2

Though these resolutions would have been largely toothless in practice.

3

Dates may be off by +/- 1 day based on the state of the AAA page as I was fetching data this morning.

item.title: The blue wave is mostly in red states. That’s a little weird.
item.description: Still Counting EP3. Plus some quick thoughts on that NYT poll in Maine.
item.content:encoded:
Still Counting Episode 3 is out. Video version above, audio below. We’ll be publishing these each week here at the newsletter. But for faster access, please subscribe on YouTube or follow us on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.

We tape Still Counting on Wednesday late mornings, and then shoot to get the episode turned around by Wednesday late afternoon/early evening. When I publish the episodes here at the newsletter, I’ll aim to add more context, but Silver Bulletin work tends to pile up midweek, so that will often take until Thursday morning.

Either way, we sincerely appreciate all the support you’ve shown for the show, and reviews, comments, likes and subscribes remain very much appreciated.

The context: Polling has been great for Democrats. But is it too good to be true?

A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll out this morning had some disappointing news for Democrats, with Susan Collins leading Troy Jackson by 3 points in Maine.

Other NYT polls had Democrats ahead by 5 points in Michigan and New Hampshire. Still, this poll feels like a “heat check” for Democrats. Since Labor Day, Democrats have been zooming ahead in FLIPR along with pretty much every model or polling average or prediction market that you might want to look at. At times, it’s literally been hard to find contrary data points to the hypothesis of a huge D sweep. So the poll serves as a reminder that picking up four Senate seats is never easy.

The NYT is a very honest (and highly-rated) pollster that doesn’t herd. So a variety of interpretations are possible:

  1. Noise/sampling error;

  2. Collins being particularly tough to beat;

  3. Democrats’ polling strength being concentrated in red states, not blue states.

The third interpretation is the one I want to briefly explore here.

For full access to FLIPR and the rest of Silver Bulletin’s midterms coverage, please consider becoming a subscriber.

As Galen, Clare and I discussed, there’s a pretty obvious bull case for Democrats. Polls have shown Democrats massively overperforming in red states, especially in the Midwest. And there’s a coherent story behind that:

  • The groups that swung most toward Trump since 2016 — namely white working-class voters and Hispanics — are finally souring on him, as you might expect for a president with a -23 net approval rating. Trump’s approval ratings weren’t great in 2018, but they were better than this: a mere -12 at this point in the election cycle. And that was a good midterm for Democrats anyway. So maybe now the bottom is falling out, and exactly those areas where Trump has made the biggest gains since 2016 are now the most vulnerable for Republicans.

  • In the heartland, this is exacerbated by extremely high gas and diesel prices, putting some surprising states like Iowa and Kansas in play.

  • And maybe there’s a bit of a throw-the-bums out mentality. As we’ve observed, being the incumbent party — which Republicans are in most of the key races — has been as much of a disadvantage as an advantage in recent elections.

By contrast, though, Democrats’ polling has been pretty “mid” in blue states.

Sure, maybe Collins, as one of the few truly moderate members left in Congress, is an exception to the throw-the-bums out mood. The other NYT polls were perfectly fine for Democrats. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed had led by 3.3 points in the FLIPR polling average prior to the NYT poll, so the poll should actually help him. The poll is consistent with El-Sayed paying a progressive “tax” of a few points, but probably still winning.

In some ways, it’s more surprising to see Chris Pappas only ahead by 5 points in New Hampshire — or Peggy Flanagan in a close-ish race in Minnesota, or Kathy Hochul struggling to achieve a double-digit lead in New York. (Though other polls disagree there.)

So if you take the polls at face value, we’re seeing a blue wave that’s … overwhelmingly concentrated in red states. As I wrote, there’s a coherent story behind it. And the evidence for it has been consistent enough that it probably has to count as the “base case”.

But there’s also some risk here for Democrats. Precisely those groups with whom they’re making the largest gains are those where polls have most overestimated Democrats in recent years.

There are also potentially huge, lopsided rewards. If the map is reverting more to something pre-Trump-like, that was a map where Barack Obama won Iowa and Ohio twice. Meanwhile, in the House, Republican gerrymanders in states like Florida and Texas were implicitly premised on the GOP having made permanent gains among Hispanics. If those are even partly undone, the Florida map in particular could turn into a dummymander. Our Lite (“polls only”) forecast for the House is probably the best way to envision this — look at that big, asymmetric right tail for Democrats. Those are basically 1994-style maps in reverse in which Democrats break through to districts where they had no business competing.

But this is potentially a somewhat boom-or-bust story for Democrats. The bear/bust case is probably less about them losing Minnesota or New Hampshire than about those gains in red states being a mirage.

I’m sure we’ll write about this more in the coming weeks.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • I mentioned that midweeks are busy. That’s partly because we’ve traditionally updated our NFL products, ELWAY and QBERT, on Wednesdays. Like FLIPR, ELWAY is a very “data-hungry” model, and wrangling all that data is a chore. AI tools help with exactly this kind of thing, so we’re hoping to get to the point where the turnaround is faster: perhaps one update Tuesday/Wednesday and then another on Friday or Saturday with the results of the Thursday Night game + injury updates. It might take a couple of weeks to get there, and we don’t want to pinky-swear promise anything until after the midterms are over. Automating things almost always helps in the long-run, but it can take more time in the short term. We’ve also toned down ELWAY’s injury adjustments, as we think those may have been picking up on some residual context that didn’t pertain to injuries themselves. (Teams that have a lot of injuries often also have a lot of other things that are going wrong.)

  • Eli wrote yesterday about whether the ostensible Republican fundraising advantage is as meaningful as headlines sometimes imply that it is.

  • And I wrote about the effect of diesel prices on the map.

  • I also wrote about why expert ratings are so much less bullish for Democrats than polls, models and prediction markets. The Maine poll is a valid reason for concern for Democrats. I’m not sure that the expert ratings are.

item.title: Why did Ohio stop being a swing state?
item.description: Still Counting EP4 covers the Ohio and Maine Senate races. Plus, we’re reviving Silver Bulletin Subscriber Questions (SBSQ).
item.content:encoded:
I’ll cover this again under “Silver Bulletin news and notes.” But I wanted to alert subscribers that we published a Model Talk on Tuesday night that evidently landed in a lot of people’s spam folders (including mine). We think it’s an important story, providing historical context on midterm elections that helps to explain FLIPR’s increasingly optimistic forecast for Democrats. So I’m going to play one of my “in case you missed it” cards and recommend you check it out.

Subscribe now

We don’t want Still Counting to be solely about the polls and the horse race. And we’ll hopefully have a chance to exhibit the show’s breadth … after the midterms. But for now, we’re in crunch time, with the election less than five weeks away. This week, Clare, Galen and I focused on two key Senate races: Maine and Ohio. We also talked about the minor scandal1 surrounding Mary Peltola’s treatment of her staffers in Alaska. I don’t think any of us expect this to be a major electoral problem for Peltola, but we differed on how newsworthy the story is.

Video above, audio version below. Once again, we are deeply appreciative of your reviews, comments, likes and subscribes.

The context: A blue wave might revive Ohio’s status as a competitive state

Pop quiz. Which Senate seat are Democrats more likely to flip: Ohio or Maine?

This might seem like an easy question. In 2024, Kamala Harris won the Pine Tree State by 7 points, but lost the Buckeye State by 11. If you buy FLIPR’s forecast, though, Ohio is actually the slightly easier pickup for Democrats.

It’s a close call, so don’t necessarily expect this to hold through Election Day. But for now, Sherrod Brown is ahead by 5.0 points in our Ohio polling average, while Troy Jackson is up by a more modest 2.7 points in Maine. FLIPR’s interpretation of the “fundamentals” (especially the presidential voting data I described above) tightens the difference in the advanced versions of our forecast, but not enough to close the gap entirely.

But FLIPR’s forecast is logical enough. In 2018, the previous Trump midterm, Brown won reelection by a healthy 6.8-point margin in a political environment we expect to be similar to what the parties will face this November. Brown lost by 3.6 points in 2024, a considerably worse year for Democrats, but he greatly outperformed Harris, who lost by 11.2. The math here seems fairly simple: the projected swing toward Democrats is considerably greater than Brown’s margin of defeat in 2024. Indeed, a fair percentage of Ohio voters evidently still think that Brown is an incumbent senator. It’s obviously not a sure thing, but this is not one of those forecasts that gives me the keeps-me-up-at-night, existential dread that I might have, say, in Texas.

In Maine, we’re navigating with much less of a reliable roadmap. Not only has Susan Collins massively outperformed the state’s partisan lean in presidential races — Maine hasn’t voted Republican for president since 1988 — she’s also massively outperformed polling averages, particularly in 2020. And Jackson's late replacement of Graham Platner was unusual, though almost certainly an improvement for Democrats given the magnitude of the accusations against Platner.

I owe you a Model Talk on what happens if Democrats lose one of the Senate races in a blue state — either Maine, where they’re on offense, or Michigan (or less likely, Minnesota or New Hampshire2) where they’re defending currently D-held seats. Would this imply that Republicans are almost certain to hold the Senate, or would Democrats still have some backdoor paths? We’ll save that for another time, because today I want to focus on Ohio.

In 2004, an election with interesting parallels to 2024, Ohio was the tipping-point state. John Kerry lost it by 2.1 points, actually slightly narrower than his 2.5-point margin of defeat to George W. Bush nationally. Had Kerry prevailed in Ohio, he would have won the Electoral College.

But Ohio is nowhere near the tipping point now. Barack Obama won it in 2008 and 2012, albeit by slightly less than his national margins of victory. In the three Trump elections, however, Ohio was 10 to 12 points more Republican than the country as a whole. Here’s that data, with a comparison between Ohio and its Big Ten neighbors, Pennsylvania and Michigan.

It’s slightly interesting that Ohio, Michigan and Pennsylvania all moved closer to the national margin in 2024. Nov. 5, 2024 was obviously not a great night for Harris, but one silver lining for Democrats is that the Electoral College vs. popular vote gap declined as compared to 2016 and 2020. Still, all three Big Ten states have become much redder in the Trump Era — but Ohio more so than the others.

After 2016, there was a much-derided journalistic cliché about reporters visiting Trump voters in Youngstown, Ohio diners. But the thing was … that was actually kind of a data-driven project. Youngstown’s Mahoning County voted for Obama by 28 points in 2012. By 2024, it went for Trump by 9 points instead. It seems like a good use of journalistic resources to cover what a swing that large looks like on the ground.

In fact, a belt stretching northeasterly across Ohio from the Kentucky to the Pennsylvania borders has seen some of the biggest red shifts in the country. Central and northwestern Ohio have also swung toward Trump, but by margins that are much more in line with Michigan and Pennsylvania.

There are a few things going on here. Nothing in Michigan (where I grew up) is Appalachian, or otherwise remotely Southern, but southeastern Ohio fits that definition. Then again, considerable parts of Pennsylvania are both literally and culturally Appalachian too, and they haven’t swung as much.

So part of this may also reflect, in a way that’s similar to fellow ex-swing state Florida, a death spiral of sorts stemming from how Democrats have given up on Ohio in presidential elections. (Or at least how Joe Biden and Harris did; Hillary Clinton intensively campaigned there in the closing days of 2016.)

In a way, though, that’s bullish for Brown and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, who has also emerged with a lead over Vivek Ramaswamy in FLIPR’s polling average. Democrats’ voter-targeting efforts are plausibly more efficient and effective than the Republican ones under Trump. In 2020 and 2024, it didn’t make much sense for Democrats to focus resources on Ohio. This year it does: Ohio is currently the third-most likely tipping-point state in the Senate after Texas and Maine, with an 11 percent chance of deciding who wins the chamber.

There are some other factors in play, too. In Ohio, Democrats have lost a massive amount of ground in the southeastern/Appalachian portion of the state — but it also matters that there have been few places in the state, other than Columbus and its northern suburbs, to counteract this. The Philadelphia suburbs have become much bluer, by contrast, and they have much more impact on the statewide vote count because the Philly metro area is about 3x more populous than the Columbus MSA.

In Michigan, Democrats are helped by favorable trends for the party in the western portion of the state. Cities like Grand Rapids are a bit unusual, with a lot of Dutch-American heritage, and they’re highly educated. Meanwhile, up toward Traverse City, the northwestern portion of the Lower Peninsula has become a somewhat hipster-ized and boutique-y getaway destination (and sometimes a primary place of residence) for older college-educated professionals elsewhere in the Midwest.

None of that means Ohio is likely to recover its swing state status in 2028. But whoever gets elected to the Senate this year will serve through the entirety of the next presidency. Democrats have a candidate with a strong electoral track record in Brown, strong enough that he’s almost a quasi-incumbent. A loss there might be just as devastating to the party’s hopes of retaking the Senate as one in Michigan or Maine.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

  • I’m not sure why Tuesday’s Model Talk landed in many subscribers’ spam folders. It was a meaty, substantive column that has been popular with people who read it. We’re talking with Substack about the issue and hope to have more detail for you within a few weeks. Honestly, Silver Bulletin is in a bit of a weird state right now where about half our traffic comes from the email list and about half from the web.3 Our email open rates are decent-to-good for a mature newsletter, and we think carefully about how many emails to send out — though we have a fair number of readers who are only interested in our sports coverage or who are not at all interested in sports. (If you’re in either of those categories, there’s a guide for you here on how to control what gets sent to your inbox.) But models like FLIPR and ELWAY are explicitly designed with the web in mind; they’re updated frequently and there’s no way to magically revise a chart in something we sent over email. If you seem to be missing Silver Bulletin posts — we’re publishing approximately 3x a week now, plus updating the models basically every day — we’d recommend that you check your spam folder and whitelist us if they’re winding up there. We may have more tips about this in the near future. Email is great for a niche publication, but spam detection algorithms can be fickle and from our perspective, frustrating.

  • We’re now aiming to update our NFL interactives, ELWAY and QBERT, twice a week instead of once a week. Generally, you should look for one update on Tuesday or Wednesday, and then the second on Friday or Saturday, reflecting the results of the Thursday Night game plus current injury and weather reports.

  • For our sports-centric subscribers, we also published the latest update to our NBA Future of the Franchise rankings on Monday.

  • Silver Bulletin Subscriber Questions (SBSQ) has been dormant since April. This wasn’t really a planned outage, but SBSQ got triaged amidst “Wet Hot Model Summer”. (We basically published COOPER, PELE, FLIPR and ELWAY consecutively without much downtime.) We’ve started a thread here to revive SBSQ for October.

For full access to FLIPR and our other models, please consider becoming a paying subscriber.

1

Or “scandal,” depending on your point of view.

2

Both states look more vulnerable at this point than Georgia, where Democrats have an incumbent running in Jon Ossoff, who is way ahead in the polls.

3

And a smaller portion from the Substack App.

item.title: The Democrats’ AI primary is heating up
item.description: The 2028 nomination race begins as soon as the midterms are over. Some Democrats like Gavin Newsom are scrambling to reformulate their positions.
item.content:encoded:
By Eli McKown-Dawson

Here at Silver Bulletin, we’ve been predicting that AI would become one of the most salient political issues for quite some time. That hasn’t happened with the general public quite yet — just 1 percent of respondents in the latest wave of Gallup’s most important problem poll named “advancement of computers/technology” as the nation’s most important issue. But over the past month, political elites have latched onto the issue in a big way, and there are growing signs that voters are following them.

Sure, some politicians, such as Bernie Sanders, had already been focused on AI — and data centers are increasingly making news and widely disliked. But some combination of the Hugging Face incident1, Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon’s comments on existential AI risk, and Dario Amodei’s subsequent essay on “pacing the frontier” have pushed the issue into mainstream political discourse. “Dozens of lawmakers are now touting new proposals to regulate artificial-intelligence models that have stepped up their capabilities,” according to the Wall Street Journal, and House Democrats are now considering creating a select committee focused on AI.

For his part, Donald Trump is something of an “accelerationist” who has called AI safety concerns a hoax. Some of his most memorable recent statements on the subject include “Whoever wins AI, wins!” and “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” He’s also staunchly pro-data center.

But not everyone is so bullish on AI, and with the arguably alarming rate at which the models are improving, this issue is likely to become more relevant before 2028. Whoever wants to be the next president will need to stake out a clear position before primary season kicks off. Those primaries might feel a long way off, but remember, candidates will almost certainly start to announce their bids in early 2027.2

We were originally going to cover what all of the presidential hopefuls were saying about AI in a single article, but with big prospective fields on each side, we’re going to split things by party. On the Democratic side, there’s broad consensus that data centers should pay for their own energy, and that federal regulation and government oversight of frontier labs are needed. The debates are more about how heavily to restrict data center construction and how aggressively to pursue a slowdown.

We’re going to focus on the top eight presidential contenders, as approximately defined by the betting markets and polls.3 To put some numbers on their positions, we’ve scored all eight candidates from 0-10 on two axes.4 The first ranges from pro-acceleration (10) to pro-regulation (0), the second from “Likes to talk about AI” (10) vs. “not much to say on the issue” (0). We’ll show each candidate's scores in their section, and include a chart for all eight candidates at the end of the post.

Silver Bulletin is a reader-supported publication. For full access to our midterms model as well as to our other AI coverage, consider becoming a subscriber.

Gavin Newsom

Acceleration: 4.5

Salience: 7.5

We’ve written about Newsom’s declining primary fortunes: he’s dropped from 37 percent in the markets last November to around 15 percent today. But he’s uber-ambitious, so there’s a good chance he’ll still run — unless, he claims, Kamala Harris jumps into the race. If he does enter the primary, Newsom will likely position himself as a leader on the AI issue due to his experience governing the state that houses the major American labs.

But in his continuous quest to optimize his political profile, Newsom has somewhat flip-flopped as the public has polarized against data centers and AI more generally.

In 2024 alone, Newsom signed 17 AI-related bills into law. But he also vetoed SB 1047, an ambitious bill supported by many people in the AI safety space, which would have created whistleblower protections and required risk assessments from developers of the most powerful AI models. And in 2025, Newsom vetoed legislation that would have required data centers to track their water usage, a move that Trump might approve.

But fast forward one year, and he’s criticizing Trump and the federal government for doing too little to regulate AI and positioning California as a regulatory trendsetter. “The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation,” he said in a recent press release.

Last year, Newsom also signed a new bill, SB 53, which had many similarities to SB 1047. It required frontier labs to publish transparency reports, disclose critical safety incidents, and maintain anonymous channels for whistleblowers. More recently, he signed a slew of bills that gave local officials more authority to monitor data centers, established a framework for independent safety evaluators, and created a state registry of AI auditors. On X, he said: “We’re making sure these companies pay the costs they create instead of sticking working families with the bill.” He also issued an executive order last month to explore, among other things, creating a “kill switch” for the most advanced models.5

Still, few other Democrats on this list have Newsom’s track record of opposing major AI regulations in the past.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

Acceleration: 1

Salience: 6

The markets are getting more bullish on an AOC primary win, although in a recent New York Times interview, she said she’ll make a decision on running after the midterms. But AOC’s AI positions have been quite consistent. Across a number of bills, she’s been Sanders’ House counterpart on the pause/moratorium side of the AI and data center debate. She signed on to Sanders’ recently proposed bill that would ban artificial superintelligence and co-led the introduction of a bill that would halt new data center construction until more federal safeguards were put in place.

Her press release when that bill was announced read, in part, “Congress has a moral obligation to stand with the American people and stop the expansion of these data centers until we have a framework to adequately address the existential harm AI poses to our society.” In addition to highlighting ICE’s use of AI, AOC has focused in on the privacy angle:

“We must sound the alarm now — because this surveillance of the American people is not going to stop. We must stop it. All of this harm has occurred, not in spite of, but because of the absence of federal legislation to regulate AI.”

On the same front, she authored the DEFIANCE Act, a bipartisan bill that would allow people depicted in explicit deepfakes to take civil action against the creators or distributors of those images. And just last week, she unveiled a new bill, along with Sanders and Jeff Merkley, that would prohibit federal use of license plate readers and cut off federal grants to state and local governments that use them.

AOC is also concerned about a potential AI bubble and said in an email to supporters that “We must make it clear now that should the A.I. bubble pop, Congress should not bail out Big Tech.” She also thinks that the “biggest threat to humanity are the tech oligarchs themselves.” We’d argue that there’s some tension between being concerned that AI is a bubble, which can imply skepticism about AI capabilities, and putting a premium on safety concerns. This is a subtlety that could split the left from the center in the primary.

Jon Ossoff

Acceleration: 3.5

Salience: 5.5

While Ossoff is getting just 8 percent support in the primary polls, on average, he’s had a recent surge in prediction markets. In 2023, he chaired a hearing on AI and human rights, but Ossoff’s foray into the data center policy debate has been more recent. Back in January, Axios reported that he hadn’t “veered into [the data center] issue — yet.” But a few months later, he launched an inquiry into whether data centers are increasing Georgia power bills. Ossoff still touted the “over $4.5 billion in AI-related venture capital investments” flowing into the state, but his concern was that, “without proper safeguards, higher prices and capital costs from increased energy generation could be passed onto Georgia families.”

That’s a fairly measured approach as compared to some of the other presidential hopefuls you’ll see on this list. But after the ongoing bout of concerning behavior from frontier models, Ossoff has become one of the more safety-focused Democrats. At a recent rally, he said:

“A capable president would move swiftly to secure and reassure the American people. Rush inspectors into frontier labs, fortify the nation against bioterrorism, demand legislation from Congress and lead the world toward an AI treaty.”

Ossoff also criticized Trump’s more laissez-faire approach: “They’ve invested heavily in AI labs. They’ve invested heavily in data centers. So, the first family has a financial stake in this industry, and as a result, the president of the United States is compromised.” At the same time, he was one of four Senate Democrats who voted to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act, a bill “aimed at pressuring state utility regulators to reduce data center-related costs,” according to Roll Call. Additionally, in August, Ossoff announced an investigation into risks AI could pose to children.

Kamala Harris

Acceleration: 4

Salience: 4

It’s still unclear whether the former vice president will throw her hat in the ring again. But given her near-universal name recognition, Harris would at least be a serious early contender, especially with South Carolina kicking off Democrats’ primary calendar. She’s currently leading in the Race to the WH primary polling average, though prediction markets are more skeptical about her chances.

Harris was the Biden administration’s unofficial AI czar. Despite that, she’s had less to say about the issue than some of the other contenders and has generally taken a middle-of-the-road approach relative to her Democratic peers. In a 2023 London speech, she said that “President Biden and I reject the false choice that suggests we can either protect the public or advance innovation; we can and we must do both.” At the same time, she warned that “when people around the world cannot discern fact from fiction because of a flood of A.I.-enabled mis- and disinformation, I ask: Is that not existential for democracy?” She also announced the US AI Safety Institute — now renamed the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence — in the same speech.

Then last month, Harris joined other Democrats in calling for more government regulation of AI and a slowdown of frontier development, including independent federal oversight and treaties with other countries to prevent dangerous uses of AI:

“The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development. A slowdown is critical in order to ensure AI serves the public interest.”

But still, she said that a slowdown “does not mean giving up on this technology’s potential to produce life-saving benefits in fields like medicine.” And Harris endorsed Project Blueprint, a project led by Democratic megadonor and venture capitalist Ron Conway to “assert influence over national AI policy.” As Nate wrote, this is an arguably slightly “weird read” on the public’s mood, treating AI as more of a “normal technology” that will be regulated through competing, partisan lobbying efforts.

Andy Beshear

Acceleration: 4

Salience: 4.5

The markets like Beshear relative to his current standing in the polls. Like Newsom, he’s had some opportunities to deal directly with data centers as a governor. Beshear has been more consistently pro-regulation, but isn’t for an outright ban. Back in June, he said “Any data center that wants to look at Kentucky is going to have to pay for 100 percent of its own energy.” He’s also said that they must pass all of Kentucky’s environmental rules and “need to be able to tell the community, and then prove to us, that they’re not going to have environmental harms.”

Originally, these restrictions took the form of pledges made to Beshear by developers. A Kentucky bill that would have required data centers to cover their own costs got stalled in the state Senate. But in early August, Beshear signed an executive order mandating that data center developers meet the above standards.

Prior to the recent round of AI news, he hadn’t said much about frontier models. But last month he joined other Democrats in calling for increased federal oversight — although with an equivocal statement that also touted the technology’s ability to make medical breakthroughs.

“AI plus CRISPR could solve every genetic disease that we know of in our lifetime, and that’s something we all want to see. But it could also cause huge job displacement. It could create national security concerns, so we have to address it.”

Still, he did call for strong federal oversight and negotiations with China on an AI agreement. A spokesperson for Beshear told the New York Times that Beshear “supports legislation that would require A.I. companies to grant the government real access to provide effective oversight.”

Pete Buttigieg

Acceleration: 4

Salience: 6

Buttigieg has hovered around 5 percent on the markets for some time. Compared to others in his party, he was relatively early to comment on potential AI-driven economic shocks. In June 2025, in a Substack post titled “We are Still Underreacting on AI,” Buttigieg compared the changes brought about by AI to “the Enlightenment or the Industrial Revolution” and said that

“Each facet of life will become very different — and the biggest difference of all is that this time, the changes will play out not over the course of generations but rather in less time than it takes an American student to complete high school.”

In an NPR interview around the same time, he said “the economic implications are the ones that I think could be the most disruptive, the most quickly. We’re talking about whole categories of jobs. Not in 30 or 40 years, but in three or four, half of the entry level jobs might not be there.”

Buttigieg has been comparatively light on discussing data center regulation, but he is concerned about wealth concentration. His signature proposal is an AI dividend, where everyone in the country would receive a share of the profits from major AI labs. “Why shouldn’t we all get a share [of the value created by AI] instead of it going to a handful of super wealthy people who are consolidating their power?” he said on a 2025 podcast.

But Buttigieg does seem to take the risk from frontier models seriously. Earlier this year, he said that AI required “a new social contract” and in September, he said “There needs to be a kill switch on rogue AI.”

Josh Shapiro

Acceleration: 5

Salience: 5.5

Like Buttigieg, Shapiro is also hovering around 5 percent on the prediction markets, but he’s actually trailing Buttigieg in the polls. The Pennsylvania governor’s evolution on data centers over the past few years looks strikingly similar to Newsom’s. Back in 2024, Shapiro touted AI investment in Pennsylvania, and in 2025, he announced that the state was “all in on AI.” “This is what a united front looks like to win the battle of AI supremacy,” he said after Amazon chose to build two datacenter campuses in PA.

But earlier this year, he released new guidelines for data center developers in the state, who must commit to “bringing their own power generation… strict transparency standards and direct community engagement… [and to] hire and train local workers.” A few months later, he described data center companies as “greedy” and “predatory” and signed an executive order that tied previous voluntary standards to tax benefits and expedited permitting:

“I’m here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers. We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers for these big tech companies. We have a long history in Pennsylvania of industry running roughshod over our communities to make a buck. That stops with me.”

On the models front, Shapiro recently called for more regulation: “I want to be clear: I am not a doomer. I don’t think it is inevitable that AI is going to take over the world or that someone will misuse it to kill us or do harm. But I do have real concerns… I’ve called on the federal government to step up and regulate the AI industry.” And earlier this year, his administration also sued Character.AI, alleging that one of their chatbots claimed to be a licensed medical professional in Pennsylvania.

Mark Kelly

Acceleration: 6

Salience: 7

The last candidate on our list, Kelly has been one of the more legislatively active Democrats on AI — and one of the more bullish on the technology. In September, he told Politico “I do believe there are benefits, and they could be significant. I also see the national security implications of not getting this right and not being the leader. This thing can blow up on us — not literally, but blow up metaphorically — at any moment and cause some real damage. We want to be ahead of it.”

Back in 2025, Kelly released an AI for America plan “that would require tech companies to contribute to a fund intended to help society adjust to the technology’s impact on jobs, infrastructure and the environment.” And last month, he proposed the Make AI Work for Americans Act that would support workers as AI changes the economy, funded through taxes on excess profits, digital advertising, and AI usage.

“These companies are getting rich off of a technology trained on the wealth of humanity’s research, knowledge, and work — our ideas and discoveries. My bill would require them to give some of that wealth back to us by investing in the American worker through an AI Horizon Fund.”

Aside from worker protections, Kelly joined other Democrats in criticizing Trump’s hands-off approach: “While the people inside the industry discuss catastrophic damage and the chance that AI, and I quote, ‘will kill us all by the end of the decade,’ the White House is actively lobbying against regulation.” Still, Kelly has played up race dynamics with China more than most Democrats, recently saying “we can’t allow the Chinese to win the race to getting the best AI technology. That would be a mistake.” He also introduced a bill that would direct the NSA to “develop and disseminate security guidance to protect America’s advanced technology from foreign adversaries.”
